newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Berlusconi offers olive branch on reform.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Berlusconi offers olive branch on reform.

text.p: Opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi voiced readiness on Wednesday to reach a compromise on constitutional reform in a statement that appeared to augur well for an ambitious attempt to give Italy stable government.

The media billionaire and conservative former prime minister told reporters he saw scope for an agreement by a cross-party commission of 70 parliamentarians who are examining potentially revolutionary changes to the way Italy works.

The commission, formed from both houses of parliament, began work in February and is about to enter a crucial final month in which its members will vote on proposed reforms to the country's weak and inefficient political system.
Its most difficult task will be to propose how a prime minister should be selected and what powers to grant the government, with parties still divided over the best blueprint.
"We have shown a readiness from the start to achieve a concrete result on institutional reforms," Berlusconi, leader of the centre-right Freedom Alliance bloc of parties, said.
"As to the solutions that should be adopted, I believe that you can also accept other people's points of view. We must make every effort, everyone must temper his own positions," he said.

The bicameral commission, chaired by Berlusconi's chief political party adversary, leftist Massimo D'Alema, is debating proposals to end a tradition of revolving-door government that has given Italy 55 cabinets since the end of World War Two.
Deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni, a member of D'Alema's PDS party, depicted the challenge on Wednesday as fundamental to Italy's hopes of joining Europe's planned single currency.
"A country's reliability is not provided only by respect for economic parameters," Veltroni told La Stampa newspaper.
"The (financial) markets also judge us on the stability of our government, on the certainty that a government chosen by the people will have the time it needs to enact its programme".

The reform drive is the third attempt of its kind in 15 years and the proposals that emerge from the commission will require several more months of debate in the full parliament and a referendum, probably in mid-1998.

The latest quest has been lent added impetus by the virtual collapse of Italy's old governing order in corruption scandals from 1992 to 1994 and growing pressure in the affluent north for federal devolution of the highly-centralised state.
The 1948 constitution was crafted to ensure no one could ever again be as powerful as Fascist dictator Benito Mussolini.
The two houses of parliament, the 630-seat Chamber of Deputies and the 315-member Senate, duplicate each other, making legislative action a snail's pace process.

Members of the commission are virtually agreed that the new Italy should have a 400-member lower house responsibile for most law-making and a 200-member upper house with a more regulatory brief and regional representatives.
It is also discussing radical proposals to devolve substantial powers to Italy's 20 regions, including those to raise taxes, and changes to the justice system.
The greatest gap between Berlusconi's bloc and the governing centre-left coalition is over the role of prime minister.
At present, the head of state appoints the prime minister who has no direct mandate from voters and can be ousted with relative ease by parliament.
Both blocs want a clearer popular designation of the prime minister through the ballot box but differ over how explicit the mandate should be and the extent of a government's powers.
Berlusconi's hard-right ally Gianfranco Fini is the most vociferous proponent of a strong system of presidential government.

Political commentators cautioned on Wednesday against ignoring Fini's role in the bargaining process and focusing only on whether Berlusconi and D'Alema, leaders of the two biggest political parties in Italy, could compromise.
"The compromise, if there is one, will have to be between three people and not two," Corriere della Sera newspaper said.
